# Section A — Multiple Choice

### Question 1

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Behavioural outcome of D1 knockout**?

- **A.** Heroin self-administration has little effect on DAT protein but dramatically reduces DAT mRNA.
- **B.** D1 and D2 receptor knockout mice are insensitive to the locomotor- stimulating effects of psychostimulants such as cocaine. Mutant mice that overexpress DA transporter show an exaggerated locomotor response to amphetamine.
- **C.** (Haber et al, 2000) Progressive recruitment of dorsolateral striatum in drug use Spiraling nigrostriatal loops mediate the intrastriatal shift The precise molecular mechanism of the intrastriatal shift is unknown, but a reduction in the dopamine transporter (DAT) may play a role Earlydrugseeking Latedrugseeking VTA Ventral Striatum SNc Dorsolateral CONTROL HEROIN USER (Yuan et al, 2015) (Liang et al, 2014) We looked further into the DAT phenomenon?.
- **D.** Used to detect a specific protein. Proteins are first separated by size.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
D1 and D2 receptor knockout mice are insensitive to the locomotor- stimulating effects of psychostimulants such as cocaine. Mutant mice that overexpress DA transporter show an exaggerated locomotor response to amphetamine.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A drug can elevate extracellular dopamine without producing its usual behavioral effect if a necessary receptor-mediated step is missing. The receptor-knockout examples therefore help test the contribution of D1- and D2-related signaling to stimulant-induced locomotion.

The lecture also contrasts transporter overexpression and amphetamine responsiveness, reinforcing that both the presynaptic transporter and postsynaptic receptor machinery matter. These are different experimental manipulations, not interchangeable ways of “removing dopamine.” The key's generalization should be read in the context of the reported locomotor endpoint. Failure of that response does not establish that every effect of the drug, every dopamine function, or every compensatory mechanism has disappeared.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).
:::

### Question 2

Which statement correctly describes **Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system**, rather than the nearby topic **Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR**?

- **A.** NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
- **B.** Motor impulsivity (impulsive action). Impaired response inhibition/inhibitory control.
- **C.** Impulsivity scales and questionnaires. Barratt impulsiveness scale (BIS).
- **D.** Cognitive impulsivity. Delay discounting.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The central noradrenergic system is an anatomical projection system, whereas an adrenergic autoreceptor is one molecular feedback mechanism within it. The locus coeruleus and related brainstem groups provide norepinephrine-containing projections to many targets. DBH expression supports the transmitter identity of those neurons.

An autoreceptor detects the neuron's own released transmitter and can regulate further firing or release. The keyed option describes the origin and chemical identity of the system, not the complete receptor mechanism. The connection is that broad projection systems still require local regulation. A change in autoreceptor signaling can alter output from a neuron whose axons influence many distant regions.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).
:::

### Question 3

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Serotonin in anxiety**?

- **A.** 5-HT has a key role in regulation of anxiety. SSRIs and 5-HT1A receptor agonists are used to treat anxiety disorders.
- **B.** Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.
- **C.** Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
- **D.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
5-HT has a key role in regulation of anxiety. SSRIs and 5-HT1A receptor agonists are used to treat anxiety disorders.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture brings together pharmacological and genetic evidence for serotonin's involvement in anxiety. It describes anxiolytic effects of 5-HT1A agonists in experimental animals and increased anxiety-like behavior in 5-HT1A-knockout mice. These observations support a role for the receptor, but do not by themselves identify the responsible brain region or receptor location.

That limitation is central to the answer. A systemically administered agonist can act at both autoreceptors and postsynaptic receptors, and a whole-animal knockout has broad consequences. It would therefore be premature to conclude that one particular serotonergic projection mediates the effect. The following lecture example narrows the question by manipulating nerve terminals and examining behavior in a defined circuit.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 4

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Compounds affecting acetylcholine storage and release**?

- **A.** Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
- **B.** Enzyme. Substrate.
- **C.** ACh is loaded into synaptic vesicles by vesicular ACh transporters (VAChT). VAChT can be blocked by vesamicol – reduces amount of ACh released when neurons fire.
- **D.** Botulinum toxins A through G are produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin proteins are taken up selectively by peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, including at the neuromuscular junction and fibers innervating smooth muscle and secretory glands.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
ACh is loaded into synaptic vesicles by vesicular ACh transporters (VAChT). VAChT can be blocked by vesamicol – reduces amount of ACh released when neurons fire.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
VAChT packages acetylcholine into **synaptic vesicles**, making it available for regulated release when the terminal is activated. Vesamicol blocks this packaging step, so less transmitter can be released even if ACh synthesis and the arrival of an action potential still occur.

The lecture contrasts storage blockade with toxins affecting release itself. Botulinum toxin prevents vesicle fusion, while black widow spider venom is described as promoting massive peripheral ACh release. These are different interventions in the same signaling sequence. Identify whether the change concerns transmitter production, vesicle filling, or fusion with the terminal membrane. The keyed option concerns filling vesicles, not receptor antagonism or enzymatic breakdown of ACh after it reaches the synaptic cleft.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).
:::

### Question 5

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Glutamate toxicity in stroke**?

- **A.** Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
- **B.** They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.
- **C.** Glutamate occurs naturally in food and contributes to the umami flavor, which is essentially savoriness. Pure MSG is delicious, but glutamate is toxic, right?.
- **D.** Glutamate: ionized form of glutamic acid (an amino acid); formed from glutamine by glutaminase. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Ischemic brain damage. One mechanism of ischemia.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture connects ischemia to **excessive extracellular glutamate and injury to nearby neurons**. Loss of adequate blood supply compromises normal cellular function, and disrupted glutamate regulation can lead to prolonged activation of excitatory receptors. The preceding receptor discussion explains why sustained ion entry, especially calcium signaling under pathological conditions, can become damaging.

This mechanism motivates efforts to protect tissue around an infarct. It does not mean glutamate is the initial vascular blockage or the only pathway of ischemic damage. The clinical-treatment question is separate: even if excitotoxicity contributes to injury, blocking one receptor class must still be shown to improve outcomes safely under actual treatment conditions. That is why the next slide discusses unsuccessful NMDA-blocker trials.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

### Question 6

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Co-release of GABA is common**?

- **A.** Thalamus Thalamus.
- **B.** The lecture treats **GABAergic interneurons** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
- **D.** Many brain areas are rich in GABA. Cortex and hippocampus: GABAergic neurons are interneurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Co-release of GABA has been demonstrated for neurons that also use glycine, ACh, DA, or glutamate. In some cases there is co-expression of the vesicular transporters for multiple transmitters in the same neuron.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The co-release examples challenge a strict **one-neuron/one-transmitter rule**. The lecture describes GABA release from neurons also associated with glycine, ACh, dopamine, or glutamate. In some cases multiple vesicular transport systems coexist; in others, packaging involves transport machinery ordinarily associated with another transmitter.

Co-release does not make the two transmitters functionally identical. Simultaneous glutamate and GABA signaling can have different effects on the target cell because their receptors and conductances differ. This allows finer control than labeling a whole neuron simply “excitatory” or “inhibitory.” The evidence to look for concerns transmitter handling and release, not merely whether a molecule can be detected somewhere inside the cell for metabolic reasons.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).
:::

### Question 8

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system**?

- **A.** Impulsivity scales and questionnaires. Barratt impulsiveness scale (BIS).
- **B.** NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
- **C.** Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR.
- **D.** Motor impulsivity (impulsive action). Impaired response inhibition/inhibitory control.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
NE neurons in the brain are located in the pons and medulla, especially in the locus coeruleus (LC). All neurons in the LC express the enzyme DBH and synthesize NE.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Noradrenergic cell bodies are concentrated in brainstem groups, especially the locus coeruleus, but their projections reach many distant regions. The enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase is important because it converts dopamine toward norepinephrine synthesis and helps identify the noradrenergic phenotype.

The key concerns anatomical origin and transmitter identity. It does not imply that norepinephrine acts only in the locus coeruleus. Extensive projections allow this relatively localized system to influence arousal, sensory processing, and cognition across the forebrain and other targets. The lecture also connects it to familiar catecholamine mechanisms—vesicular storage, reuptake, metabolism, and tonic or phasic activity—so anatomy and transmitter handling should be understood together.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).
:::

### Question 9

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Identifying the precise anxiety-modulating mechanism**?

- **A.** Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
- **B.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.
- **C.** Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT) neurotransmitter used by serotonergic neurons. Serotonin is an indoleamine.
- **D.** Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Are anxiety-regulating 5-HT1A receptors postsynaptic or presynaptic?. Experiments show that excitation of the serotonergic nerve terminals (increases 5-HT release) had an anxiolytic effect – increased time in open-arm of elevated plus-maze; inhibition of the terminals was anxiogenic.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The experiment narrows the anxiety question by manipulating **serotonergic nerve terminals**, rather than simply administering a drug throughout the body. In the lecture's account, terminal excitation increases serotonin release and increases open-arm time in the elevated plus-maze; terminal inhibition produces the opposite, anxiety-like pattern.

The lecture interprets this evidence as supporting a contribution from postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors in the studied circuit. The logic is that increasing transmitter delivery to target cells reduces the measured anxiety-like behavior, rather than reducing transmitter output through autoreceptor inhibition. Keep the scope specific: open-arm time is a behavioral index, not a direct report of subjective anxiety, and the finding does not establish that every serotonergic projection has the same function.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 10

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **The cholinergic pharmacology of Botox**?

- **A.** Choline is taken back up by choline transporters; transporters can be blocked by hemicholinium-3 (HC-3) – ACh production declines.
- **B.** Botulinum toxins A through G are produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin proteins are taken up selectively by peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, including at the neuromuscular junction and fibers innervating smooth muscle and secretory glands.
- **C.** Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
- **D.** Enzyme. Substrate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Botulinum toxins A through G are produced by the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin proteins are taken up selectively by peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals, including at the neuromuscular junction and fibers innervating smooth muscle and secretory glands.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The essential mechanism is **presynaptic inhibition of acetylcholine release**. Botulinum toxin enters peripheral cholinergic terminals and disrupts the machinery needed for synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane. At a neuromuscular junction, reduced ACh release means less stimulation of the muscle's nicotinic receptors, producing weakness or paralysis.

This explains why a toxin can also have carefully controlled therapeutic uses in conditions involving excessive muscle contraction. The molecular action is not the same as blocking the muscle receptor directly or inhibiting ACh breakdown. The answer's bacterial origin and uptake description identify the substance, but the release-to-muscle-response chain explains the effect. The course examples describe pharmacological principles, not instructions for handling or administering the toxin.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).
:::

### Question 11

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **NMDA receptor blockers in stroke**?

- **A.** Glutamate occurs naturally in food and contributes to the umami flavor, which is essentially savoriness. Pure MSG is delicious, but glutamate is toxic, right?.
- **B.** Glutamate: ionized form of glutamic acid (an amino acid); formed from glutamine by glutaminase. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters.
- **C.** Vesicular glutamate transporters move glutamate into synaptic vesicles: VGLUT1 or VGLUT2 or rarely VGLUT3; found only in glutamatergic neurons. In some neurons, these transporters are expressed with markers for 5-HT, DA, ACh, or GABA, indicating that glutamate is a co-transmitter.
- **D.** They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
They don’t seem to work… JAMA. 2001;285(13):1719-1728. doi:10.1001/jama.285.13.1719 2001;286;(21):2673-2682. doi:10.1001/jama.286.21.2673.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture contrasts a **plausible neuroprotective mechanism with disappointing clinical trial results**. NMDA receptors participate in excitotoxic processes, so blocking them seemed a reasonable strategy for limiting ischemic injury. However, the historical trials cited on the slide did not establish the hoped-for clinical benefit.

This does not prove that NMDA receptors play no role in the injury mechanism. It shows that mechanistic involvement is not sufficient to demonstrate that a particular treatment improves patient outcomes. The supplied slide does not give enough information to attribute failure to one specific cause, such as dose, timing, or adverse effects, so those explanations should not be invented. Interpret “they don't seem to work” within the trials and course context, not as a current universal treatment guideline.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 25. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

### Question 12

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **GABAergic projections: direct and indirect pathway Direct**?

- **A.** Thalamus Thalamus.
- **B.** The lecture treats **GABAergic interneurons** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** GABAA receptor—ionotropic; GABAB receptor—metabotropic (more later). GABAA receptor is composed of five subunits, usually two α subunits, two βs, and one γ.
- **D.** Muscimol: GABAA orthosteric agonist from the mushroom Amanita muscaria. Bicuculline: competitive antagonist for GABAA receptors; blocks binding of GABA; if taken systemically, causes convulsions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Thalamus Thalamus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The direct and indirect basal-ganglia diagrams illustrate **inhibition and disinhibition across a chain of connections**. In the simplified direct pathway, striatal inhibition of an inhibitory output region can reduce its inhibition of the thalamus, facilitating motor-related signaling. The indirect pathway involves additional connections that can increase inhibitory output and restrain that signaling.

The key “Thalamus Thalamus” is a figure-label extraction error, not a meaningful answer. A useful explanation must trace the sign of each connection rather than assume that activating any GABAergic neuron suppresses every downstream region. The Parkinson's comparison then shows how altered dopamine input changes the balance of these pathways. This item needs substantive choices before it can validly assess the circuit concept.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).
:::

### Question 13

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **DAT protein DAT mRNA Effectof heroin exposureon striatalDATproteinandmRNA**?

- **A.** self-administrationreducestheexpressionofDATmRNAin striatalastrocytes.
- **B.** Used to record activity from a group of neurons. Neurons express a fluorescent sensor such as GCaMP.
- **C.** Heroin self-administration has little effect on DAT protein but dramatically reduces DAT mRNA.
- **D.** The striatum has no DAT mRNA of VTA dopamine neuron origin Which cell of striatal origin expresses DAT? VTA dopamine neuron We bet on astrocytes. DAT DAT mRNA.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Heroin self-administration has little effect on DAT protein but dramatically reduces DAT mRNA.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The reported result is a mismatch between two measurements: striatal DAT protein changes little, whereas measured DAT mRNA is markedly reduced after heroin self-administration. Protein abundance and transcript abundance are not interchangeable, so this is not automatically a contradiction.

The lecture uses the mismatch to motivate questions about cellular origin and anatomical location. Protein in an axon terminal can originate from synthesis in a cell body elsewhere, while locally measured RNA may belong to another cell population. The key should therefore be interpreted as the specific result presented in the lecture, not a universal finding for every heroin exposure. The next step is to identify which cells contribute to each measurement.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).
:::

### Question 14

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR**?

- **A.** Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR.
- **B.** Motor impulsivity (impulsive action). Impaired response inhibition/inhibitory control.
- **C.** Impulsivity scales and questionnaires. Barratt impulsiveness scale (BIS).
- **D.** Cognitive impulsivity. Delay discounting.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Adrenergic receptors include several subtypes with different signaling functions. The lecture highlights the inhibitory autoreceptor role of alpha-2 receptors: when activated on a norepinephrine neuron, they can reduce further transmitter output through effects on firing or release.

This is negative feedback, not a statement that every adrenergic receptor suppresses activity. Alpha-2 receptors can also occur at other locations, where their functional consequences depend on the receiving cell. The existing key names “the autoreceptor” but does not identify the mechanism. The useful distinction is between a receptor detecting the neuron's own transmitter to regulate output and a receptor on a different target cell mediating that cell's response.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).
:::

### Question 15

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Serotonin in hunger and eating**?

- **A.** Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT) neurotransmitter used by serotonergic neurons. Serotonin is an indoleamine.
- **B.** The lecture treats **Tryptophan hydroxylase** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **C.** Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
- **D.** Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Serotonin influences hunger and eating behavior. Neurons in AN secrete α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP).
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The feeding example distinguishes **appetite-suppressing and appetite-promoting signals** within hypothalamic circuitry. The lecture describes arcuate-nucleus neurons associated with α-MSH and others associated with NPY and AgRP. Their projections reach the paraventricular nucleus, where melanocortin signaling contributes to the regulation of feeding.

α-MSH activates MC3/4 receptors and favors appetite suppression; AgRP antagonizes those receptors and favors feeding. This receptor opposition explains more than saying that serotonin “controls hunger.” Serotonin can influence the balance within the circuit, but the downstream peptides and receptors determine how that influence is expressed. The lorcaserin example belongs to the course's historical pharmacology discussion; it should not be interpreted here as a current prescribing recommendation.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 16

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase**?

- **A.** Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
- **B.** Enzyme. Substrate.
- **C.** Choline is taken back up by choline transporters; transporters can be blocked by hemicholinium-3 (HC-3) – ACh production declines.
- **D.** Preganglionic neurons of both branches of the autonomic nervous system are cholinergic, as are the ganglionic neurons of the parasympathetic system. Norepinephrine is the transmitter of the sympathetic ganglionic neurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) breaks ACh down to choline and acetic acid; four subunits combine to form a tetramer (G4). Three forms of AChE:.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Acetylcholinesterase terminates cholinergic signaling by **hydrolyzing ACh to choline and acetic acid**, as described in the lecture. Rapid removal matters at neuromuscular junctions because continuing receptor stimulation would interfere with the separation of successive contractions and relaxation.

The slide distinguishes soluble and membrane-associated enzyme arrangements, including the specialized form at the neuromuscular junction. Their positioning helps bring enzyme and released transmitter together efficiently. Reversible AChE inhibitors have the opposite effect from blocking ACh release: they prolong the availability of transmitter that has already been released. The dementia examples illustrate that mechanism in the course; they do not mean that these drugs restore lost neurons or reverse every cause of cognitive impairment.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Glutamate biosynthesis**?

- **A.** Glutamate uptake: 5 different excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs) occur in different locations. Astrocytes express EAAT2 and may account for about 90% of total glutamate uptake in the brain.
- **B.** High levels of extracellular glutamate are dangerous; EAAT2 knockout mice develop seizures and have short life spans.
- **C.** Glutamate: ionized form of glutamic acid (an amino acid); formed from glutamine by glutaminase. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters.
- **D.** Vesicular glutamate transporters move glutamate into synaptic vesicles: VGLUT1 or VGLUT2 or rarely VGLUT3; found only in glutamatergic neurons. In some neurons, these transporters are expressed with markers for 5-HT, DA, ACh, or GABA, indicating that glutamate is a co-transmitter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Glutamate: ionized form of glutamic acid (an amino acid); formed from glutamine by glutaminase. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Glutaminase converts **glutamine to glutamate**, supplying part of the transmitter pool used by glutamatergic neurons. Glutamate is also an amino acid with metabolic roles in many kinds of cells, so its mere presence in a cell does not establish that the cell releases it as a neurotransmitter.

The lecture distinguishes the specialized transmitter pool from these other biochemical functions. Glutamatergic neurons must also package glutamate into vesicles and release it at appropriate terminals. Do not confuse glutaminase with glutamine synthetase: the latter converts glutamate into glutamine in astrocytes, helping recycle material back to neurons. The two enzymes support opposite steps in a shared neuron–glia cycle rather than performing the same reaction.

### Question 22

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **What happens to the byproducts of ACh catabolism**?

- **A.** The neuromuscular junction. a special type of synapse.
- **B.** Basal forebrain cholinergic system (BFCS): neurons in several brain areas; origin of cholinergic innervation of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic system structures. Cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (LDTg and PPTg) project to the basal ganglia and thalamus; others to the lower brainstem and spinal cord.
- **C.** Choline is taken back up by choline transporters; transporters can be blocked by hemicholinium-3 (HC-3) – ACh production declines.
- **D.** Preganglionic neurons of both branches of the autonomic nervous system are cholinergic, as are the ganglionic neurons of the parasympathetic system. Norepinephrine is the transmitter of the sympathetic ganglionic neurons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
Choline is taken back up by choline transporters; transporters can be blocked by hemicholinium-3 (HC-3) – ACh production declines.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The recycled molecule is **choline**, not intact acetylcholine. AChE first breaks released ACh down in the extracellular space. Choline transporters then return choline to the terminal, where ChAT can use it with acetyl-CoA to synthesize new transmitter.

Blocking choline uptake with hemicholinium-3 reduces precursor availability and therefore reduces subsequent ACh production. This differs from the monoamine examples in which the transmitter itself is taken back up by a transporter such as SERT or DAT. It also differs from inhibiting AChE, which slows transmitter breakdown rather than limiting precursor recycling. A complete explanation follows the cycle from release to hydrolysis, precursor uptake, and resynthesis instead of calling every transport process “ACh reuptake.”

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

### Question 23

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Vesicular packaging of glutamate**?

- **A.** EAAT1: highly expressed in astrocytes in the cerebellum. EAAT3: major neuronal glutamate transporter; postsynaptic localization.
- **B.** Vesicular glutamate transporters move glutamate into synaptic vesicles: VGLUT1 or VGLUT2 or rarely VGLUT3; found only in glutamatergic neurons. In some neurons, these transporters are expressed with markers for 5-HT, DA, ACh, or GABA, indicating that glutamate is a co-transmitter.
- **C.** Glutamate uptake: 5 different excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs) occur in different locations. Astrocytes express EAAT2 and may account for about 90% of total glutamate uptake in the brain.
- **D.** High levels of extracellular glutamate are dangerous; EAAT2 knockout mice develop seizures and have short life spans.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Vesicular glutamate transporters move glutamate into synaptic vesicles: VGLUT1 or VGLUT2 or rarely VGLUT3; found only in glutamatergic neurons. In some neurons, these transporters are expressed with markers for 5-HT, DA, ACh, or GABA, indicating that glutamate is a co-transmitter.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
VGLUT proteins transport glutamate into **synaptic vesicles**. They are therefore markers of the capacity for vesicular glutamate signaling, not enzymes that synthesize glutamate or transporters that remove it from the extracellular space. EAATs perform the latter uptake function.

The co-transmission examples qualify an overly rigid “one neuron, one transmitter” rule. A cell identified by dopamine, serotonin, ACh, or GABA markers may also express a VGLUT and release glutamate. In the VTA example, the lecture describes dopamine and glutamate release from separate vesicles at different terminal types. Thus, co-expression does not imply that the two chemicals necessarily occupy the same vesicle or are released identically at every synapse of that neuron.

### Question 24

- **A.** GABAA receptors are sensitive to CNS- depressant drugs such as benzodiazepines (BDZs), barbiturates, and ethanol, which act as positive allosteric modulators – they enhance the action of GABA on the receptor. Other positive modulators:.
- **B.** BDZs and ethanol can only modulate receptor activity, regardless of dose; high doses of barbiturates, anesthetics, and neurosteroids can open the receptor channel even in the absence of GABA. BDZs such as diazepam (Valium) increase effect of GABA on a receptor; diazepam alone has no effect, confirming that BDZs are positive allosteric modulators and not receptor agonists.
- **C.** GABAA receptor—ionotropic; GABAB receptor—metabotropic (more later). GABAA receptor is composed of five subunits, usually two α subunits, two βs, and one γ.
- **D.** Muscimol: GABAA orthosteric agonist from the mushroom Amanita muscaria. Bicuculline: competitive antagonist for GABAA receptors; blocks binding of GABA; if taken systemically, causes convulsions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: C.**
GABAA receptor—ionotropic; GABAB receptor—metabotropic (more later). GABAA receptor is composed of five subunits, usually two α subunits, two βs, and one γ.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
GABAA receptors are **ligand-gated ion channels**, commonly assembled from five subunits. In the adult-neuron example used by the lecture, opening the channel permits chloride conductance that inhibits the postsynaptic cell. GABAB receptors, by contrast, work through G proteins and indirect effects on channels and signaling pathways.

The common two-α, two-β, one-γ arrangement is a useful example, not the composition of every GABAA receptor. Differences in subunits help explain why receptor populations respond differently to modulators such as benzodiazepines, anesthetics, and neurosteroids. The central distinction is receptor mechanism: rapid channel-mediated inhibition versus metabotropic inhibition. Do not mistake the receptor family name for the enzyme GAD or the uptake transporters GATs.

### Question 27

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **A point of clarity**?

**Correct answer: A.**
Dopamine-deficient (DD) mouse: gene for TH is knocked out but not the gene for DBH – NE can be synthesized but not DA. A functional TH sequence is placed under DBH regulatory control A point of clarity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The important detail is the **selective restoration of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)**, not simply the presence of the dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) gene. TH performs the first step in the catecholamine synthesis pathway. Removing TH would otherwise prevent the production of dopamine and the norepinephrine made from it. Placing a functional TH sequence under DBH regulatory control restores synthesis in cells that normally make norepinephrine.

Dopaminergic cells do not receive this restoration, so they remain dopamine deficient. The opening slide clarifies the model from the preceding lecture. The key's first sentence is incomplete without its second sentence: an intact DBH gene alone cannot compensate for a missing upstream precursor. This is a genetic manipulation of synthesis, not blockade of a dopamine receptor.

Likewise, identifying a neuron as cholinergic does not by itself tell you whether it is sympathetic or parasympathetic. Trace CNS → autonomic ganglion → target organ, and label the transmitter at each connection. The key summarizes the course's general arrangement; it should not be used as an exceptionless inventory of every peripheral autonomic pathway.

EAATs remove glutamate from the **extracellular space**, limiting the duration and spread of excitation. Astrocytic EAAT2 has a particularly prominent role in the lecture's account, illustrating that transmitter inactivation is not exclusively a job for the presynaptic neuron.

Glutamate taken into astrocytes can subsequently enter the glutamate–glutamine recycling pathway. The approximate uptake percentage in the key expresses the course's emphasis on astrocytes; the mechanistic distinction is more important than treating that number as universal. VGLUT fills vesicles, EAAT removes extracellular transmitter, and glutamine synthetase performs an intracellular chemical conversion.

The lecture associates medial and dorsolateral/dorsomedial prefrontal systems with attention, planning, executive control, and the inhibition of actions. Orbitofrontal systems are emphasized for action–outcome relationships, reward value, and updating choices when circumstances change.

The keyed option identifies the first grouping. The distinction helps explain why response inhibition and delay-related choice are not necessarily the same deficit. These functions still depend on interactions with striatum and other regions; the slide is not a claim that one prefrontal area works alone. Interpret the anatomical labels as components of control networks, and match the behavioral task to the particular operation being tested.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

### Question 33

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Serotonin synthesis is regulated by enzymatic**?

- **A.** The lecture treats **Tryptophan hydroxylase** as a key concept that should be understood in relation to the surrounding mechanisms and examples.
- **B.** Serotonin synthesis can be stimulated by tryptophan or 5-HTP. Tryptophan from diet: ratio of tryptophan to other amino acid competitors for transport across blood–brain barrier determines whether serotonin synthesis is stimulated or not.
- **C.** Para-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA) selectively blocks 5-HT synthesis by irreversibly inhibiting TPH. Acute tryptophan depletion (ATD) large doses of amino acids minus tryptophan X.
- **D.** Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT) neurotransmitter used by serotonergic neurons. Serotonin is an indoleamine.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT) neurotransmitter used by serotonergic neurons. Serotonin is an indoleamine.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Serotonin, **5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT**, is an indoleamine rather than a catecholamine. Its precursor is tryptophan. Tryptophan hydroxylase first converts tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP); aromatic amino acid decarboxylase then converts 5-HTP to serotonin. The hydroxylation step is the rate-limiting step emphasized in the lecture.

The keyed option correctly identifies the transmitter and its chemical class, but a fuller understanding also requires this two-step sequence. Enzyme activity and the availability of tryptophan jointly influence how much serotonin can be synthesized. Do not substitute tyrosine hydroxylase merely because its name sounds similar: that enzyme belongs to the catecholamine pathway, whereas tryptophan hydroxylase belongs to the serotonin pathway.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
:::

### Question 34

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Acetylcholine in the somatic nervous system**?

- **A.** The neuromuscular junction. a special type of synapse.
- **B.** Basal forebrain cholinergic system (BFCS): neurons in several brain areas; origin of cholinergic innervation of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic system structures. Cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (LDTg and PPTg) project to the basal ganglia and thalamus; others to the lower brainstem and spinal cord.
- **C.** In the brain, cell bodies of cholinergic neurons are clustered in only a few areas. Interneurons in the striatum: regulation of movement depends in part on the balance between ACh and dopamine (DA).
- **D.** Nicotinic receptors—respond to the agonist nicotine, an alkaloid in the tobacco plant. Muscarinic receptors—respond to muscarine, an alkaloid first isolated from fly agaric mushrooms (Amanita muscaria).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: A.**
The neuromuscular junction. a special type of synapse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a **somatic motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber**. The motor terminal releases ACh, which activates nicotinic ACh receptors on the muscle membrane. Channel opening depolarizes that membrane and links the nervous system's signal to muscle activation.

The short keyed phrase names the junction but does not explain why it belongs to this topic. The important distinction is from an autonomic pathway, which uses a ganglionic relay to regulate organs and glands. It is also distinct from an ACh synapse between two neurons within the brain. Keep the transmitter, receptor class, and target cell together: ACh is the signal, the nicotinic receptor is the detector, and skeletal muscle is the target.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

### Question 35

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **EAAT knockout**?

- **A.** EAAT1: highly expressed in astrocytes in the cerebellum. EAAT3: major neuronal glutamate transporter; postsynaptic localization.
- **B.** Astrocyte transporters convert the glutamate they take up to glutamine using glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is then transported out of astrocytes and picked up by neurons, where it can be converted back into glutamate by glutaminase.
- **C.** Glutamate is the brain’s workhorse for fast, excitatory neurotransmission. Glutamatergic pathways in the brain include.
- **D.** High levels of extracellular glutamate are dangerous; EAAT2 knockout mice develop seizures and have short life spans.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
High levels of extracellular glutamate are dangerous; EAAT2 knockout mice develop seizures and have short life spans.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Removing EAAT2 compromises a major route for **clearing extracellular glutamate**. The lecture reports seizures and shortened survival in knockout mice, linking disrupted clearance to excessive excitation. The result demonstrates why a normally useful excitatory transmitter must be tightly regulated outside cells.

The manipulation is not equivalent to eliminating glutamate synthesis or blocking all glutamate receptors. Transmitter can still be released, but its removal is impaired. This makes the experiment informative about transport and extracellular regulation. However, a constitutive knockout affects an animal over development as well as during testing, so its full phenotype should not be reduced to the effect of one brief drug exposure. The evidence supports the importance of uptake, not an unrestricted claim that glutamate is inherently harmful.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

It also describes inverse effects at the benzodiazepine site that reduce GABA's effectiveness. ### Question 40

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Cholinergic projections in the NS**?

- **A.** In the brain, cell bodies of cholinergic neurons are clustered in only a few areas. Interneurons in the striatum: regulation of movement depends in part on the balance between ACh and dopamine (DA).
- **B.** Nicotinic receptors—respond to the agonist nicotine, an alkaloid in the tobacco plant. Muscarinic receptors—respond to muscarine, an alkaloid first isolated from fly agaric mushrooms (Amanita muscaria).
- **C.** Nicotinic acetylcholine (nAChRs) receptors: ionotropic; mediate fast excitatory responses in both the CNS and the PNS. When ACh binds, the channel opens, Na+ and Ca2+ enter the neuron or muscle cell, which depolarizes the cell membrane.
- **D.** Basal forebrain cholinergic system (BFCS): neurons in several brain areas; origin of cholinergic innervation of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic system structures. Cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (LDTg and PPTg) project to the basal ganglia and thalamus; others to the lower brainstem and spinal cord.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: D.**
Basal forebrain cholinergic system (BFCS): neurons in several brain areas; origin of cholinergic innervation of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic system structures. Cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (LDTg and PPTg) project to the basal ganglia and thalamus; others to the lower brainstem and spinal cord.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The lecture distinguishes **long-range cholinergic projection systems** from local interneurons. Basal forebrain neurons provide cholinergic input to cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic structures. Cholinergic cells in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei project to regions including the thalamus and basal ganglia.

The origin of a projection is not the same as its target. A cholinergic terminal in the cortex can belong to a neuron whose cell body lies in the basal forebrain. This organization helps explain how a relatively localized population can influence widespread neural processing. By contrast, the striatal interneurons discussed later act within a local circuit. The key is the source-to-target arrangement, not an assumption that ACh has one function in every destination.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

### Question 41

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Astrocytic metabolism of glutamate**?

- **A.** Flow of both Na+ and Ca2+. Activated by simultaneous binding of glutamate and a co-agonist: glycine or D- serine released by astrocytes.
- **B.** Astrocyte transporters convert the glutamate they take up to glutamine using glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is then transported out of astrocytes and picked up by neurons, where it can be converted back into glutamate by glutaminase.
- **C.** Glutamate is the brain’s workhorse for fast, excitatory neurotransmission. Glutamatergic pathways in the brain include.
- **D.** AMPA receptor, named for selective agonist AMPA; most fast excitatory responses to glutamate are mediated by stimulation of AMPA receptors. Kainate receptor, named for selective agonist kainic acid.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Astrocyte transporters convert the glutamate they take up to glutamine using glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is then transported out of astrocytes and picked up by neurons, where it can be converted back into glutamate by glutaminase.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The recycling sequence is **uptake into astrocytes → conversion to glutamine → transport to neurons → reconversion to glutamate**. Glutamine synthetase catalyzes the astrocytic conversion; glutaminase catalyzes the neuronal conversion. This couples removal of released transmitter to replenishment of the supply used for later signaling.

There is a wording problem in the original key: transporters do not themselves convert glutamate into glutamine. The lecture's shorthand should be distinguished from the clearer account in Chapter 8, which assigns transport to EAATs and conversion to the enzyme glutamine synthetase. Keeping movement and chemical transformation separate makes the cycle intelligible and explains how astrocytes support both signal termination and continued neurotransmission.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).
:::

The source reports that DAT deletion in VTA neurons only partially reproduces the effect of an organism-wide DAT knockout on dopamine reuptake. This comparison motivates a question about the remaining clearance capacity and whether astrocytic DAT contributes to it.

### Question 45

Which statement best matches the lecture discussion of **Uptake of dietary tryptophan**?

- **A.** Reducing brain 5-HT using the ATD method seems to impair memory consolidation of verbal information but has little or no influence on working memory or attention (Mendelsohn et al., 2009). ATD also induced a negative cognitive bias, and reduced sleep duration and quality (Cools et al., 2007).
- **B.** Serotonin synthesis can be stimulated by tryptophan or 5-HTP. Tryptophan from diet: ratio of tryptophan to other amino acid competitors for transport across blood–brain barrier determines whether serotonin synthesis is stimulated or not.
- **C.** Para-chlorophenylalanine (PCPA) selectively blocks 5-HT synthesis by irreversibly inhibiting TPH. Acute tryptophan depletion (ATD) large doses of amino acids minus tryptophan X.
- **D.** Tryptophan loading: administration of pure tryptophan. Dietary:.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Correct answer: B.**
Serotonin synthesis can be stimulated by tryptophan or 5-HTP. Tryptophan from diet: ratio of tryptophan to other amino acid competitors for transport across blood–brain barrier determines whether serotonin synthesis is stimulated or not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The relevant quantity is not simply how much tryptophan a meal contains, but **tryptophan relative to the other large neutral amino acids competing for transport into the brain**. More circulating tryptophan may not increase brain entry if competing amino acids increase at the same time. Brain entry affects the precursor available to tryptophan hydroxylase and therefore can influence serotonin synthesis.

The lecture uses a low-protein, high-carbohydrate meal to illustrate this ratio. In its account, insulin promotes uptake of competing amino acids into peripheral tissues, increasing tryptophan's relative access to transport. The point is a transport-and-synthesis mechanism, not a guarantee that a particular meal will produce a predictable mood change in every individual.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).
